steps.title: Draw the smallest piece
steps.instruction: Run the smallest building block by itself.
steps.explain: This is the piece that remains when the pattern stops subdividing. Check it before adding calls that repeat it.
steps.expected: One building block of the pattern.
steps.question: Which commands actually leave a mark?
steps.answer: Trace the drawing commands. Turns and movements with the pen up prepare the next mark.
steps.help: Check the changed lines first. Keep parentheses and commas in place. Indent each line inside a loop or function by four spaces.

steps.title: Test the stopping case
steps.instruction: Add the function and its small test call together. Run before increasing the number of levels.
steps.explain: A recursive function calls itself with a smaller problem. The stopping condition ends the repetition. Start with that case to see the smallest piece.
steps.expected: One smallest piece of the pattern. Compare it with this step’s preview.
steps.question: Which condition stops this function from calling itself again?
steps.answer: Find the if condition near the beginning. The recursive calls move their input toward that stopping condition.
steps.help: Check the changed lines first. Keep parentheses and commas in place. Indent each line inside a loop or function by four spaces.

steps.title: Add one recursive level
steps.instruction: Change only the test call. Predict how many pieces will appear, then run.
steps.explain: The function reaches its recursive calls once more before reaching the stopping case. Each call makes a smaller copy.
steps.expected: The next level of the pattern. Compare the number and size of pieces.
steps.question: How many smaller calls does one call make?
steps.answer: Count the calls to the function inside its own body. Follow one down to the stopping condition.
steps.help: Check the changed lines first. Keep parentheses and commas in place. Indent each line inside a loop or function by four spaces.

steps.title: Test one repeat
steps.instruction: Build one example using the value shown. Run and inspect it.
steps.explain: side has one value in this test. Follow how it controls the drawing before putting the commands in a loop.
steps.expected: One visible example from the group. Check its position, size, and color.
steps.question: Where is side used in the drawing code?
steps.answer: Find the variable in the movement, size, or color expressions. A different value changes those instructions.
steps.help: Check the changed lines first. Keep parentheses and commas in place. Indent each line inside a loop or function by four spaces.

steps.title: Make a second example
steps.instruction: Add a second example. Look for the lines you repeated.
steps.explain: Both examples use the same drawing instructions. Only an input value changes. You can put that repeated work in a loop.
steps.expected: Two examples from the group. Compare their positions or sizes.
steps.question: Which lines are identical in both examples?
steps.answer: The drawing instructions match. A loop can reuse them for each value.
steps.help: Check the changed lines first. Keep parentheses and commas in place. Indent each line inside a loop or function by four spaces.

steps.title: Repeat the whole group
steps.instruction: Replace the trial examples with this loop. Run the whole program again.
steps.explain: for side in range(3): takes one value at a time. Indent the repeated body four spaces. The first line after the loop returns to the left edge.
steps.expected: The complete group. Compare it with the first example you tested.
steps.question: What changes if the loop has fewer values?
steps.answer: The body runs fewer times. range(n) supplies n values, starting at 0.
steps.help: Check the changed lines first. Keep parentheses and commas in place. Indent each line inside a loop or function by four spaces.

steps.title: Draw the next line
steps.instruction: Replace the practice call with the project code below, then run.
steps.explain: goto(x, y) chooses a position: x moves left or right; y moves up or down. penup() lets you reposition without a connecting line. pendown() draws the next movement.
steps.expected: The new line or connected edges at the coordinates in this block.
steps.question: What happens if you leave the pen down while moving to a new starting point?
steps.answer: A connecting line appears between the previous position and the new one.

steps.title: Check the complete drawing
steps.instruction: Run the completed program. Compare its shapes and details with the finished example.
steps.explain: The complete program combines the pieces you have tested, in drawing order.
steps.expected: A complete outward-facing Koch snowflake with recursive edges

steps.nav: Make a change and explain it
steps.title: Make a change and explain it
steps.instruction: Choose one input in a function call or loop. Predict its effect, change it, and run. Then try a second change.
steps.explain: Change one thing at a time so you can connect the result to the exact line you edited.
steps.expected: Your own version of Koch Snowflake.
steps.question: Which line changed your drawing, and why?
steps.answer: Point to your edit, name the input you changed, and compare the result before and after.
